source: Liu, Geng, Wu, Sucholutsky, Lombrozo, Griffiths (2025, ICML) Mind Your Step (by Step): chain-of-thought can reduce performance on tasks where thinking makes humans worse
finding: Gap 8. Six tasks where verbal thinking hurts humans were tested with chain-of-thought (CoT). CoT hurt models in three of them (implicit grammar learning, face recognition, learning labels with exceptions) and gave mixed results in the other three. None of the six tasks is an insight problem, so this is indirect evidence only.
numbers: Artificial grammar: o1-preview 57.7% vs GPT-4o 94.0% on a 440-item subset (36.3 pp drop with CoT). GPT-4o full set 87.5% direct vs 64.4% CoT (23.1 pp). Face recognition: all 6 vision-language models worse with CoT (GPT-4o 64.0% to 51.2%; Claude 3 Opus 44.0% to 29.6%). Exceptions task: GPT-4o needed 2.9 rounds direct vs 12.5 with CoT (+331%). Spatial intuition (water-glass tilt): no significant change (GPT-4o 38% vs 40%). Inconsistency detection: CoT helped (up to +40 pp on some sets).
quote: CoT reduces performance in tasks where deliberation hurts humans
limits: Insight items (matchsticks, riddles, CRA) were not used. Models and humans fail for different reasons. Effects vary by model; Claude 3.5 Sonnet was nearly flat on the grammar task (65.9% vs 67.7%).
agent_relevance: The human finding that verbalising hurts is not a safe guide for LLMs. Test step-by-step versus direct on the actual S6 insight items, per item type, before deciding that operator steps should be silent or written.

source: Gema et al. (2025, TMLR) Inverse scaling in test-time compute
finding: Gap 4/8. Longer reasoning can lower accuracy in reasoning models. Claude models get more distracted as they think longer; o-series models resist distractors but overfit to familiar problem framings; all models lose accuracy on constraint-tracking (zebra) puzzles in the natural-length setup.
numbers: Misleading Math: Claude Opus 4 falls from nearly 100% to about 85-90% as reasoning length grows. DeepSeek R1 natural-length setup: 70% down to 30% with five distractors. o3 stable in the controlled setup but with shorter traces. Zebra puzzles (200 items, BBEH): all models show inverse scaling in the natural overthinking setup. 2,500 questions per misleading task, 500 per distractor count.
limits: Not insight tasks. Tasks were built to produce inverse scaling, so the rate on ordinary items is not estimated. Reasoning length was set by prompt keywords in one setup.
agent_relevance: Reasoning length is not a clean explanation of the NazoNazo gap (7.6% vs 17.6%). A longer trace can help or hurt by task; hold the token budget equal when comparing insight operators.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling: familiar framing effect (Misleading Math with well-known framings)
finding: Gap 10. Models that recognise a famous puzzle framing (birthday paradox, Sleeping Beauty) apply a memorised complex solution to a trivial question. Reasoning traces show the model naming the famous puzzle. Adding distractors that hide the framing restored the right answer.
numbers: Trace evidence: models state they recognise a variant of a known paradox, then run the memorised method. When extra distractors make the puzzle unrecognisable, o3 focuses on the trivial question. The effect persists when the model sets its own reasoning length.
quote: models explicitly recognize these familiar framings
limits: Qualitative trace reading plus accuracy curves; per-model rates are in figures and were not recorded here. Not about insight puzzles directly.
agent_relevance: Famous insight puzzles (nine-dot, candle, matchsticks) may trigger recalled solutions, not reasoning. Score S6 on altered variants where the memorised answer is wrong.

source: Liu, Chen, Pang, et al. (2025, COLM) Understanding R1-Zero-like training: a critical perspective
finding: Gap 7. The 'Aha moment' is already present in the base model before RL. DeepSeek-V3-Base writes 'Aha' and 'wait' on MATH questions. After R1-Zero training, self-reflection occurs more often but is not positively correlated with higher accuracy. Keyword detection and LLM-based detection of self-reflection disagree, so counts depend on the detector.
numbers: 500 MATH questions, 8 responses each, DeepSeek-V3-Base-685B hosted by the authors; a question counts as showing self-reflection if at least 1 of 8 responses does. The paper reports reflection is more frequent in R1-Zero but not tied to higher accuracy (its Sec. F; exact correlation figures not recorded here).
limits: Math only. Open models. The keyword pool excludes 'wait' because it can be incidental, so numbers depend on the pool.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'wait' or 'Aha' as a signal of insight in the agent's trace. Score restructuring from content change plus outcome, not from marker words.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Beyond the 80/20 rule: high-entropy minority tokens drive effective RL for LLM reasoning
finding: Gap 7. Only a minority of tokens in a reasoning trace have high entropy, and these 'forking tokens' include words such as 'wait', 'however', 'unless'. They steer which path the model takes. Training with only the top 20% highest-entropy tokens matches or beats full training; training on the lowest 80% hurts.
numbers: About 50.64% of tokens have entropy below 1e-2; about 20% of tokens carry high entropy. Qwen3-8B matches full-gradient updates with 20% of tokens; larger models gain more. Raising temperature on forking tokens only improves AIME 2024/2025 scores.
limits: Qwen3 open models; math. It links marker words to entropy but does not test whether a marker predicts correctness for one trace.
agent_relevance: Entropy at the marker position, not the word itself, is the useful signal. Log token entropy around any switch-frame step in the agent before using a marker as a trigger.

source: Chen et al. (2025, Anthropic) Reasoning models don't always say what they think
finding: Gap 5/9. Reasoning traces often do not mention the factor that actually changed the answer. Models use a hint in at least 1% of cases but verbalise it in under 20% of those cases for most settings. Outcome-based RL raises faithfulness at first, then plateaus low.
numbers: Overall faithfulness 25% for Claude 3.7 Sonnet and 39% for DeepSeek R1 across 6 hint types; 20% and 29% on misalignment hints. Faithfulness plateaus at 28% on MMLU and 20% on GPQA after outcome RL. Traces are less faithful on harder tasks.
limits: Multiple-choice hint insertion, not riddles. Faithfulness is judged only for hint use.
agent_relevance: A written trace is not proof of what drove the answer. A required 'check each candidate' step may be written without being used. Verify by a behaviour test (does the final answer change when the check fails?).

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning models know when they're right: probing hidden states for self-verification
finding: Gap 5. Hidden states of reasoning models encode whether an intermediate answer is correct. A linear probe predicts correctness well and is calibrated, even before the answer is fully written. Using the probe to stop reasoning cuts tokens with no accuracy loss. Models encode correctness yet do not use it.
numbers: In-distribution probes: ROC-AUC above 0.7 on all datasets and ECE below 0.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B above 0.9 ROC-AUC on AIME. Early exit with the probe cut inference tokens by 24% with no accuracy loss.
limits: Open distilled reasoning models; math and logic data; probes need weights, so they do not apply to closed models. Out-of-distribution transfer was weaker on harder data.
agent_relevance: Supports a design where the verification signal is separate from the generating chain. The NazoNazo verification failure (a correct candidate was written but not endorsed) fits this picture.

source: Huang et al. (2024, ICLR) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Gap 1/9. Without an oracle, asking a model to review and revise its answer lowers accuracy. Earlier gains came from knowing when the answer was already right. A 'try again' prompt turns correct answers into wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7 over two self-correction rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 84.3, CommonSenseQA 89.7; GPT-4 GSM8K 97.5, HotpotQA 59.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K.
limits: 2023-era models; 100 to 200 test items in some tables; not reasoning-trained models. Later reasoning models may differ.
agent_relevance: An always-on reconsideration step is not free. Any 'switch frame' operator needs a trigger that fires mostly on wrong answers, and must be tested for flips of correct answers.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022, Anthropic) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Gap 9. Larger models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions in the right format. They can estimate P(True) for their own proposed answer and be trained to predict P(IK), the chance that they know the answer. P(IK) rises when relevant material or hints are in context. Calibration of P(IK) on new tasks is weaker.
numbers: Abstract-level reading only; exact calibration error values were not recorded in this pass.
limits: Pre-reasoning-model era; no insight or riddle tasks. Did not test whether confidence tracks speed or sudden solution.
agent_relevance: Gives a baseline for agent confidence on riddle items: elicit P(True) after the answer and compare with accuracy across the S6 set. Human Aha ratings predict accuracy (Salvi); test the same for model confidence.

source: McCoy, Yao, Friedman, Hardy, Griffiths (2023) Embers of autoregression
finding: Gap 10. Model accuracy depends on how probable the task, the input and the target output are, even when the task is deterministic. Low-probability cases fail more. This predicts that rare or novel puzzle answers will be harder than famous ones, separate from any insight demand.
numbers: GPT-4 decoding a shift cipher: 51% when the output is a high-probability word sequence vs 13% when low-probability. Eleven tasks, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4.
limits: 2023 models. Not insight tasks. Shows a confound: the answer's probability, not the need for restructuring, may drive difficulty.
agent_relevance: Match S6 items on answer probability, or the result mixes insight difficulty with phrase rarity. Use the same answer-word frequency band for insight and control items.

source: Golchin & Surdeanu (2024, ICLR) Time travel in LLMs: tracing data contamination
finding: Gap 10. A cheap black-box method finds benchmark contamination: give the dataset and split name and the start of an item, and see if the model completes the rest. It agreed with human experts on whether a model was contaminated 92% to 100% of the time over 14 dataset partitions. GPT-4 showed contamination for AG News, WNLI and XSum; GPT-3.5 only for the XSum test split.
numbers: Seven datasets, 14 partitions, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; agreement with human experts 92-100%. GPT-4 flagged on test partitions of AG News and WNLI and the XSum test split; IMDB and RTE only train splits.
limits: Tested on classification, NLI, summarisation; not puzzles. Needs the benchmark name in the prompt. Does not separate exposure from memorisation of answers.
agent_relevance: Run this completion test on every S6 item (guided versus general instruction) before use. An item the model can finish from its first words should be dropped or rewritten.

source: Danek, Fraps, von Mueller, Grothe, Oellinger (2014, Frontiers) It's a kind of magic: what self-reports can reveal about the phenomenology of insight
finding: Gap 6. Magic tricks work as an insight task. People watched 34 trick videos up to three times, tried to find the method, and said yes or no to an Aha. Insight was defined by self-report. The authors argue that insight problems 'per se' do not exist; any problem can be solved with or without insight depending on prior knowledge.
numbers: 34 tricks; 48 analysed participants (50 recruited); 1,632 trials. 49% of trials solved; 51% unsolved or dropped for familiarity. For 41% of solved tricks, participants reported an Aha. Five dimensions rated at the time and again 14 days later with stable ratings; happiness rated most important.
quote: insight problems per se don't exist
limits: Small student sample. Insight is the self-report itself, so it cannot be validated against a process measure. Aha was asked only after solving.
agent_relevance: Item-level insight rate (41% of solutions) is the kind of base rate the S6 set should record. Expect many correct solutions to be non-insight even on insight-style items, for humans and probably models.

source: Salvi, Bricolo, Kounios, Bowden, Beeman (2016) Insight solutions are correct more often than analytic solutions
finding: Gap 9. In four experiments, solutions reported as insight were more often correct than analytic ones, for every task and both time windows. Analytic answers included more errors of commission and also more last-second guesses.
numbers: Exp 1 CRA (38 participants, 120 items): 93.7% insight vs 78.3% analytic. Exp 2 anagrams (51, 180 items): 97.6 vs 91.9. Exp 3 rebus (110, 32 items each): 78.5 vs 63.2. Exp 4 visual Aha (27, 50 items): 78.4 vs 41.5. Narrow window (2-10 s): 94.4/83.2, 97.6/91.8, 75.1/64.4, 68.6/43.6. Error rate in the last 5 s vs the preceding 10 s: 34.1% vs 10.5% (Exp 1). Time limit 15 s per item.
limits: Short deadlines. Insight status is self-labelled after each answer. Authors state it is unknown if results generalise from lab puzzles to real problems. Contradicted in spirit by Danek and Wiley on false insights. Read through a page summary tool, so table values are as extracted.
agent_relevance: The accuracy gap is the human benchmark an agent's self-reported 'sudden' answers must meet. Collect the agent's insight label per answer and report accuracy by label, as Salvi did.

source: Normative data for 111 compound remote associates test problems in Romanian (2019, Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Gap 6. A new RAT set was normed on 63 speakers. Item accuracy ranges widely from near 0 to near 1, so solution rate by item is a usable difficulty measure, but accuracy alone says nothing about whether insight was used.
numbers: 111 items, n=63. Mean accuracy 0.54 (SD 0.43); mean RT for correct 15.37 s (SD 10.53); mean RT all trials 22.41 s (SD 22.39). Cronbach alpha 0.93 for accuracy, 0.97 for response time. No age effect: F(2,60)=0.048, p=0.953.
limits: Norms for accuracy and RT only; no Aha ratings per item. Romanian words, so item difficulty is language-specific.
agent_relevance: Per-item human accuracy and RT should be stored with every S6 item and used to build difficulty-matched sets. Missing from this source: per-item insight rate.

source: Generative AI models outperform students on divergent and convergent thinking assessments (2025, Scientific Reports)
finding: Gap 6/10. On a 57-item Remote Associates Test, three chatbots far outscored 46 students. The authors say this questions whether standard creativity tests suit AI. The RAT is therefore close to saturated for current models and gives little signal for S6.
numbers: Humans: 19.13 of 57 correct (SD 9.96, range 2-42), about 34%. ChatGPT-4o 54.96 (SD 0.89); DeepSeek-V3 51.00 (SD 1.59); Gemini 2.0 44.93 (SD 1.88). All p<0.001. Each model run repeatedly (small SD across runs).
limits: Human time limit and test fatigue; student sample. Accuracy only, no Aha or process measure. Public RAT items may be in training data.
agent_relevance: Do not use public CRA/RAT items as the main S6 test. They are likely saturated and possibly contaminated. Use altered or newly made items with a human norm.

source: Tabatabaeian, O'Bi, Landy, Marghetis (2025, PNAS) An information-theoretic foreshadowing of mathematicians' sudden insights
finding: Gap 3. Mathematicians working on proofs at blackboards in their own departments were filmed. Verbal 'Oh I see' moments were coded as sudden insights. These moments were preceded by growing unpredictability in writing and gesturing, so even sudden insights have a measurable build-up. Insight events were rare but found in nearly every session.
numbers: 6 mathematicians, each on 2 conjectures (set theory and geometry): 12 proof sessions, 4 h 5 min in total; 4,653 blackboard interactions. 27 sudden insights across 13 of 14 proof sessions (including a pilot). Problems were hard (Putnam-level; the Putnam median score is 0 or 1 of 120).
quote: insights that appear to come out of nowhere are actually prefigured
limits: Insight is defined by what the person says. Small expert sample, one lab. Smaller insights not spoken were not counted. Shows lead-up changes, not that insight is slow in the sense of Klein.
agent_relevance: Sudden insight in real work shows an early-warning pattern. For the agent, score trace behaviour in the steps before a frame switch (rising variety of moves) as well as the switch itself.

source: Klein & Jarosz (2011) A naturalistic study of insight (abstract via Crossref; full text not available)
finding: Gap 3. 120 real insight incidents from cognitive task analysis interviews and media accounts were coded on 14 features. The result is a descriptive model different from puzzle findings, with three pathways: contradiction, impasse, and connection. Only the abstract could be read.
numbers: 120 incidents; 14 coded features; 3 pathways (contradiction, creative desperation after impasse, connection). The share of gradual versus sudden cases was not in the abstract.
limits: Abstract only. Sample is self-selected stories (interviews and media), so it is biased toward memorable incidents. No count of gradual versus sudden was seen. A 2020 safety-critical paper (PMC7550865) cites it only for Mann Gulch, as a sudden reframing.
agent_relevance: Only one of three pathways is impasse. An agent test built only on impasse puzzles covers a third of the real routes. Add contradiction-detection and connection-finding items to S6.

source: Macchi, Turco, Inglese, Caravona (2026, Journal of Intelligence) Pupil dilation and unconscious analytic thought in insight problem solving
finding: Gap 6/2. A physiological index (pupil size) was used instead of a self-report. People who later solved the problem showed constant high pupil dilation during an unrelated arithmetic incubation task; non-solvers and a control group showed falling pupil size. None solved during the first attempt.
numbers: 91 recruited; 82 analysed (aged 19-47, M=23.2). Experimental n=40: 11 solvers (27.5%) after incubation, 29 non-solvers; control n=42. Original problem form; a reformulation of this problem raised solving to 60% in earlier work.
limits: One problem, one lab, 11 solvers. Pupil size has many causes. Interpretation as unconscious analytic thought is contested by business-as-usual accounts.
agent_relevance: An objective, non-report measure of restructuring effort exists for humans. The nearest agent measure would be hidden-state or entropy signals during incubation-like steps, not the words in the trace.

source: Surprise! Clarifying the link between insight and prediction error (2024, Psychonomic Bulletin & Review)
finding: Gap 9. In a preregistered online study with compound remote associates, only the Aha dimension of surprise tracked a meta-cognitive prediction error about whether a problem was solvable. Pleasure, certainty and suddenness did not; suddenness correlated negatively. Aha is a bundle, and the parts do not move together.
numbers: Preregistered; CRA items; expected solvability rated first, then solving and Aha ratings. Surprise related to prediction error mainly on correct solutions. Sample size and effect sizes were not recorded in this pass.
limits: Effect strongest for correct solutions. Online sample. Earlier work on anagram time prediction found a link confounded by difficulty.
agent_relevance: For model self-report of 'Aha', ask about the dimensions separately (surprise, certainty, suddenness). A single 'did you have an insight' label mixes parts that can disagree.

source: d'Aliberti & Horta Ribeiro (2026) The illusion of insight in reasoning models: re-read of the forced-reconsideration experiment
finding: Gap 1/7. Re-reading shows what the +8.41 pp covers. It is the gain of a second pass with a reconsideration cue over the first pass, over all items. It is not a comparison of always-on versus uncertainty-triggered versus never at equal tokens. The text read has no cue-free second-pass control. Spontaneous mid-trace shifts are rare and often harmful. Entropy makes the cue work better.
numbers: Forced reconsideration (Table 5): MATH pass 1 32.21% -> pass 2 40.62% (+8.41 pp; 320,000 paired samples; 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong); crosswords 9.70% -> 10.15% (+0.45 pp; 83,200 pairs); RHour +0.01 pp. Spontaneous shifts: Math raw effect -7.40 pp in the high-entropy tail and -22.88 pp in the low-entropy 80%. External models: shift rates 0.00-0.25% (DeepSeek-R1) and 0.88-2.21% (GPT-4o) on MATH-500; GPT-4o accuracy lower after a shift at every temperature. Cue test (500 problems, Qwen2.5-1.5B): one SD higher entropy raised odds of a correct answer after the cue about 2.2x to 2.5x across 3 cues. Small slice: Qwen2.5-7B +5.97 pp but Llama 3.1-8B -4.19 pp.
limits: Pass 2 doubles generation cost, so equal-token tests are absent. Models are small GRPO-tuned ones plus two external models. No insight riddles or CRAs; the puzzle domains (crosswords, RHour) had near-floor accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open. A fair test needs three arms (never, always, entropy-gated) plus a cue-free resample at equal tokens on riddle-type items. The Llama result shows the cue can hurt.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo: re-read of figures, verification failure and renewable item design
finding: Gap 4/5/10. The headline numbers match on a second reading: 38 frontier models, retrieval-free, zero-shot. The paper says verification failure is hard to square with memorisation, since a memorising model would endorse the answer it already wrote. It proposes a rotating test: open, blind and post-cutoff sets.
numbers: 120-item human subset: non-reasoning models average 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%, humans 52.9% (95% CI 46.6-59.2%). GPT-5 is the exception and falls within the human CI. Verification failure among wrong answers: 5.23% (Gemini 2.5 Flash Preview) to 39.34% (Grok 4); Claude Opus 30.35%. Item sets: 42 open, 159 blind (including the 120 human items, hashes posted), plus a new set from children's books not online. Table 2 uses literal string matching of the gold answer in the thought-log, so it counts any mention.
limits: Same authors only; no independent replication found. The reasoning versus non-reasoning gap is observational and not controlled for trace length or training data. Literal matching can count answers mentioned only to reject them. A footnote warns that the GPT-5 comparison does not prove equivalence to humans.
agent_relevance: The cross-check flag on NazoNazo figures is closed. Verification failure is measured only by gold-answer mention. Use a written candidate-check step and count flips to test the fix (gap 5 stays open).

source: Alavi Naeini et al. (2023) LLMs are fixated by red herrings: Only Connect Wall - contamination statement
finding: Gap 10. The authors state that the walls are public text on fan sites, so training exposure is possible. They argue it is unlikely because model performance is low, and distributed the dataset in compressed form as a basic guard. They call leakage an open problem. Low accuracy is weak evidence of no exposure.
numbers: No contamination test run. Dataset shared in compressed format only.
limits: The argument from low performance is not a test. Later models may score higher through exposure. Compression does not stop web copies.
agent_relevance: Treat any public puzzle set as exposed. For classic insight problems use altered numbers or surface, and report a completion test as in Golchin and Surdeanu.
